content: 1. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) emphasized the need for further research to address knowledge gaps in areas where recommendations were made. Specifically, research is required to determine the true false-positive rate of the F1 Rapid Diagnostic Test (F1RDT) for both pneumonic and bubonic plague when compared to reference standards such as culture and PCR, which are considered imperfect. 2. Studies are needed to estimate the pre-test probability of plague in various scenarios, including endemic areas, non-endemic areas, and during outbreaks, for F1RDT and other diagnostic methods. 3. Research should quantify the cost-effectiveness of using F1RDT for detecting and diagnosing pneumonic and bubonic plague. 4. Efforts should be made to standardize the development of new rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) and evaluate the accuracy of second-generation RDTs. 5. Collaboration among laboratory researchers is essential to define antigen targets for new RDT development, harmonize the use of PCR, and establish a standardized diagnostic algorithm for plague, specifying the targeted genes and laboratory methods. 6. The GDG identified the need for research to determine the persistence of viability and infectiousness of Yersinia pestis in the body fluids of individuals who were infected with plague. 7. Studies should explore the risk of plague transmission associated with funeral rites for different population subgroups, including pregnant women, stillbirths, twins, and traditional leaders. 8. Research on the persistence of Y. pestis should consider the impact of antimicrobial therapy administered before death. Animal model studies may provide valuable insights. 9. The GDG recommended the development of clinical guidance and algorithms based on a syndromic approach to managing cases of plague, including both diagnosis and treatment. 10. WHO guidelines for plague management include revised recommendations for the use of rapid diagnostic tests, fluoroquinolones for case management, and personal protective equipment to prevent post-mortem transmission. 11. The document will be updated as necessary based on the results of an impact survey and feedback from health ministries and reference laboratories. WHO will collect information on survey responses and other comments within 2-3 years after publication. After three years, WHO will formally appraise emerging evidence on topics such as the use of F1RDT for diagnosis, antibiotic selection, and personal protective equipment, including feasibility issues and new medicines or technologies. 12. This information will guide the development of new topics for the guidelines and evaluate whether current recommendations and evidence summaries require updates. 13. Key questions addressed by the guidelines include whether F1RDT accurately detects plague compared to culture, PCR, or paired serology, and whether RDTs should be used to detect or diagnose pneumonic and bubonic plague in endemic areas or during outbreaks. 14. The guidelines also explore the effectiveness and safety of various antibiotics, including fluoroquinolones, streptomycin, gentamicin, doxycycline, and chloramphenicol, for treating confirmed or suspected plague cases. 15. The risk of plague transmission from exposure to the remains of individuals who died of plague is another critical area of investigation. This includes understanding the contagiousness of body fluids, the survival of Y. pestis in human remains, and documented cases of transmission through human or animal remains. 16. The guidelines aim to summarize all reported cases of plague infection occurring during post-mortem exposure to human and animal remains, providing evidence-based recommendations for prevention and control.
